delta__N.share: It appears that the share of colluding scenarios rises with patience, peaks at fairly high but not the highest patience, and then eases off, while it falls steadily as the number of firms grows. The inputs interact strongly: impatient firms in crowded markets almost never collude, most likely because each firm gets only a small slice of cartel profit while undercutting wins most of the market for a round. Among very patient firms the number of firms hardly matters, because the threat of losing future profits holds even large cartels together. The dip at the most patient end appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid: there an investigation that finds nothing wipes out ordinary earnings for good, and patient firms weigh that loss heavily.
delta__N.theta: It appears that collusion intensity rises with patience up to fairly high levels and then falls, and that it is lower the more firms there are. The peak shifts towards more patient values as the number of firms grows, most likely because larger cartels need more patience before they can hold any raised price at all. Past the peak, very patient cartels appear to moderate their prices to avoid drawing the regulator's attention, since they have more future profit to lose, with a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid adding to that fall. At the most patient end the number of firms barely changes how hard the cartel pushes prices.

delta__phi.share: It appears that collusion becomes more common as the preferenced share grows, and that it rises with patience before easing off at the most patient end. Volume that is split evenly whatever the price cannot be won by undercutting, so it most likely shrinks the reward for cheating on the cartel. That help matters most among impatient firms and almost disappears once firms are patient enough to hold the cartel together anyway. At the very highest patience the preferenced share even has a slightly reversed effect, which seems to come from small markets with a price grid and a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid.
delta__phi.theta: It appears that collusion intensity rises with the preferenced share and follows a rise-then-fall pattern in patience. The preferenced share makes the biggest difference among impatient firms, most likely because fewer of their cartels are forced to keep prices below what they would like in order to stop members cheating. Once firms are patient, the lines for different preferenced shares come together, because the temptation to cheat no longer limits the price. The fall at high patience appears to reflect patient cartels choosing caution to protect their future profits, plus the price-grid quirk.

delta__tick.share: It appears that a coarser tick size generally lowers the share of colluding scenarios, while patience raises it up to fairly high levels before it eases off. The tick cuts both ways: among impatient firms a moderate tick actually helps the cartel, most likely because undercutting by a whole price step is a big cut when margins are thin, and the price war drops below the earnings firms make in normal competition on a price grid. Among very patient firms the grid markets fall away while markets without a grid keep rising. That late fall appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid, not a real effect of patience: it disappears when every investigation ends in a conviction.
delta__tick.theta: It appears that a coarser tick size lowers collusion intensity at most patience levels, and that intensity rises then falls with patience. Without a price grid, intensity keeps rising until very high patience and then eases only a little, which seems to be genuine caution by cartels protecting their future profits. With a coarse grid it peaks earlier and drops much more, which appears to be mostly a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid. A grid also most likely forces the cartel to move in whole steps, so it cannot fine-tune a modest, less conspicuous price.

delta__slope.share: It appears that a more sensitive regulator screen sharply reduces collusion at every level of patience, making it the main deterrent in this chart. Patience raises the share up to fairly high levels, because the threat of a price war then holds the cartel together, and each screen level peaks there. The drop at the most patient end seems to come from markets with a price grid and is a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid, where an investigation that finds nothing destroys ordinary earnings that patient firms value highly; without a grid the share simply levels off.
delta__slope.theta: It appears that collusion intensity drops steeply as the screen becomes more sensitive, and that it rises then falls with patience. With no screen, colluding firms most likely go all the way to the full-collusion price, because a higher price carries no extra risk of investigation. With any screen, every extra bit of price raises the chance of an investigation that would end the cartel, and very patient cartels, having the most future profit at stake, appear to hold prices down further. Even a gentle screen seems to bite hard on how far prices are pushed.

delta__rhoTip.share: It appears that a higher tip probability reduces collusion, while patience raises it up to fairly high levels before it eases off. A whistleblower tip can start an investigation whatever the price, so the cartel cannot avoid it by pricing modestly; it most likely shortens the cartel's expected life and so weakens the hold of future profits. Patience partly offsets this, since in markets without a price grid the share with tips keeps rising as firms grow more patient. The fall at the most patient end appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid, where a tip that finds nothing wipes out ordinary earnings.
delta__rhoTip.theta: It appears that average collusion intensity falls as tips become more likely, and rises then falls with patience. The fall with tips seems to come mainly from fewer cartels forming: among cartels that do form, tips actually push prices higher, most likely because staying inconspicuous helps little when a whistleblower may expose the cartel anyway. That price-raising effect appears strongest among the most patient firms, which would otherwise be the most cautious.

delta__pEvidence.share: It appears that collusion becomes less common as investigations become more likely to find evidence, because the expected fine rises, and that patience raises collusion up to fairly high levels. Among the most patient firms the pattern dips and then recovers as evidence becomes certain. That recovery appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid: there an investigation that finds no evidence leaves firms worse off than a conviction, so more evidence looks less bad. In markets without a grid, more evidence lowers collusion steadily.
delta__pEvidence.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls as the chance of finding evidence rises, most likely because each extra bit of price then carries a larger expected fine; the effect looks strongest at moderate patience. Intensity rises then falls with patience. Among the most patient firms intensity dips and then rises again as evidence becomes certain, which appears to be the same price-grid quirk rather than real economics.

delta__fineRatio.share: It appears that larger fines steadily reduce collusion at every level of patience, as long as a screen or tip can start an investigation. Patience raises the share in every fine level up to fairly high values, most likely because the threat of a price war holds patient cartels together. When fines are small, the share drops again among the most patient firms, which appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid rather than an effect of patience itself.
delta__fineRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls as the fine grows at every level of patience, most likely because each extra bit of price raises the chance of an investigation and therefore the expected fine. Intensity rises then falls with patience in every fine level. Under very heavy fines the patience levels converge on low intensity, suggesting that once fines are severe, patience makes little difference to how far prices are pushed.

delta__sBarRatio.share: It appears that collusion peaks at middle values of the room between cost and the customers' walk-away spread, and rises then falls with patience. This seems to be the sum of opposing effects. Without a price grid, more room means the same degree of collusion produces a wider, more visible spread for the screen, so collusion falls; with a grid, a narrow room leaves few or no price steps above normal competition, so collusion rises with room. Patience lifts every room level, and the dip at the most patient end again appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid.
delta__sBarRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity peaks at a fairly narrow, but not the narrowest, room between cost and the walk-away spread, and rises then falls with patience. Without a price grid, intensity falls steadily as the room widens, most likely because the same degree of collusion is a wider spread that the screen notices more. The narrowest room is pulled down by grid markets, where a coarse grid leaves no room to collude and a finer grid offers only an all-or-nothing jump.

N__phi.share: It appears that collusion falls as the number of firms grows and rises with the preferenced share. The preferenced share helps most in crowded markets, where the temptation to undercut is greatest, because volume split evenly whatever the price cannot be won by cheating. With very few firms it makes almost no difference, or even hurts slightly, most likely because in small grid markets more preferencing raises ordinary competitive earnings, leaving less room to collude and more exposure to a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid.
N__phi.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with the number of firms and rises with the preferenced share, and the lines fan out: the preferenced share barely matters with very few firms but makes a large difference in crowded markets. This is most likely because the preferenced share eases the temptation to cheat, so fewer large cartels are forced to hold prices below the level they would prefer.

N__tick.share: It appears that collusion falls with both the number of firms and the tick size, but a coarser grid hurts much less in crowded markets. A grid seems to bring an offsetting benefit there: undercutting by a whole price step is a big cut when each firm's margin is thin, and the price war falls below normal grid earnings, so more large cartels can hold together. With very few firms only the costs show: fewer price steps to choose from, a minimum markup the screen can always see, and a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid.
N__tick.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls as the number of firms grows and as the tick size grows, with the grid cutting intensity by a similar proportion at every firm count, slightly less in crowded markets. The fall with the tick most likely reflects having to move prices in whole steps, the screen always seeing at least a full step of markup, and the price-grid quirk. The slightly smaller cut with many firms is consistent with the grid making cheating less tempting there.

N__slope.share: It appears that collusion falls both as the number of firms grows and as the screen becomes more sensitive, and these effects roughly multiply because they act through different channels: more firms make cheating more tempting, while the screen raises the risk of an investigation. The smallest firm counts look almost identical, most likely because small cartels hold together easily. The penalty for having many firms grows under steeper screens, apparently because the risk of investigation makes the future less certain, which weakens what keeps large cartels together.
N__slope.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls steeply as the screen becomes more sensitive at every firm count, and is lower with more firms. Without a screen, colluding firms most likely push straight to the full-collusion price. Under steep screens, crowded cartels cut intensity much more, apparently because high prices raise the risk of investigation, which in turn makes cheating more tempting, so large cartels must keep prices down to stay together.

N__rhoTip.share: It appears that collusion falls as tips become more likely and as the number of firms grows. Tips seem to hit crowded markets proportionally harder, most likely because a tip shortens the cartel's expected life and so weakens the hold of future profits, which matters most where the temptation to cheat is already high. In small cartels, which hold together easily, the tip mainly works through expected fines and a shorter life.
N__rhoTip.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with tips and with the number of firms, and that the proportional fall from tips is larger in crowded markets. This seems mainly to be because fewer cartels form, especially large ones; among cartels that do form, tips tend to push prices higher, since hiding helps less when a whistleblower may strike anyway.

N__pEvidence.share: It appears that collusion falls as the number of firms grows and as investigations become more likely to find evidence, and these act almost independently. This is most likely because evidence raises the expected fine but does not change the temptation to cheat, which is how the number of firms acts. The smallest firm counts look almost identical, and the curve flattens as evidence becomes certain, which appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid.
N__pEvidence.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls as evidence becomes more likely at every firm count, and is lower with more firms. The proportional fall is smaller in crowded markets, most likely because fewer large cartels collude in the first place, leaving less for deterrence to remove. The near-flat stretch at the highest evidence levels in crowded markets appears to be the price-grid quirk offsetting the extra deterrence.

N__fineRatio.share: It appears that collusion falls steeply as fines grow and also falls with the number of firms, with these acting nearly independently. This seems to be because the fine is measured against each firm's own full-collusion profit, so adding firms does not make a given fine heavier per firm. The number of firms therefore acts mainly through the temptation to cheat, while the fine acts on whether colluding is worth the risk at all.
N__fineRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with the fine at every firm count and is lower with more firms, but the gap between small and large cartels narrows sharply under heavy fines. This is most likely because heavy fines push surviving cartels to low prices, where the risk of investigation and the strain on the cartel are small, or leave only scenarios with no risk of investigation at all, so the number of firms has less to act on.

N__sBarRatio.share: It appears that collusion peaks at middle values of the room between cost and the walk-away spread for every number of firms, and falls as firms are added. The middle peak seems to blend opposing forces: without a price grid, more room makes collusion more visible to the screen, while with a grid a narrow room leaves little space above normal competition. More firms appear to scale the whole curve down by a similar proportion, as expected when the number of firms acts only through the temptation to cheat.
N__sBarRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity peaks at a fairly narrow, but not the narrowest, room for every number of firms, and falls as firms are added. Beyond that peak, intensity most likely falls because the same degree of collusion is a wider spread that the screen notices more. The narrowest room is pulled down by grid markets, where a coarse grid leaves no step at all to collude on.

phi__tick.share: It appears that collusion rises with the preferenced share and falls with the tick size. The preferenced share helps in every tick level but less with a grid, most likely because the grid already eases the temptation to cheat, leaving less for preferencing to do. In very small grid markets more preferencing also raises ordinary competitive earnings, which seems to shrink the room for a cartel and can even lower collusion.
phi__tick.theta: It appears that collusion intensity rises with the preferenced share and falls with the tick size, with these effects adding up almost independently. Without a grid, the preferenced share does not change prices, the screen or the fine, so its effect most likely comes entirely from easing the temptation to cheat, letting more cartels form and fewer hold prices down to stay together. The grid appears to lower intensity by forcing whole price steps that the screen can see.

phi__slope.share: It appears that collusion falls sharply as the screen becomes more sensitive and rises with the preferenced share, which lifts the whole curve by a broadly similar proportion. This seems to be because they do different jobs: the preferenced share decides whether a cartel can be held together, while the screen decides whether colluding is worth the risk of investigation. Moving up the chart therefore shows easier cartel discipline, and moving across shows enforcement.
phi__slope.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls steeply with screen sensitivity and rises with the preferenced share at every screen level. The proportional boost from preferencing seems larger under steep screens, most likely because a steep screen makes high prices risky, which in turn makes cheating more tempting, and preferencing relieves exactly that temptation.

phi__rhoTip.share: It appears that collusion falls sharply as tips become more likely and rises with the preferenced share, by a similar amount at every tip level. Tips seem to work by shortening the cartel's expected life, which also makes cheating more tempting, and the preferenced share acts as a counterweight by making undercutting less rewarding. Their effects therefore look nearly additive.
phi__rhoTip.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with the tip probability at every preferenced share, and that the preferenced share adds a similar amount at every tip level. The fall with tips most likely comes from fewer cartels forming, even though the cartels that do form tend to price higher when a whistleblower might expose them anyway.

phi__pEvidence.share: It appears that collusion falls as evidence becomes more likely and rises with the preferenced share, with these acting almost independently. Evidence raises the expected fine, while the preferenced share makes the cartel easier to hold together, so they most likely work on different decisions. The preferenced share helps a bit less where evidence is likely, and the flattening between the highest evidence levels appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid.
phi__pEvidence.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls as evidence becomes more likely and rises with the preferenced share in every evidence level. The boost from preferencing looks larger where evidence is unlikely, most likely because more cartels form there, so the easing of the temptation to cheat applies to more of them.

phi__fineRatio.share: It appears that collusion falls steeply as fines grow and rises with the preferenced share, by a broadly similar proportion at every fine level. The fine seems to decide whether colluding is worth the risk, while the preferenced share decides whether the cartel can be held together. With no fine, the chart mostly shows whether firms can keep the cartel from breaking apart, which is where preferencing matters most visibly.
phi__fineRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with the fine at every preferenced share, and that the advantage from preferencing shrinks to almost nothing under heavy fines. This is most likely because heavy fines leave few cartels, mostly in scenarios with no screen and no tips, where preferencing has little left to change.

phi__sBarRatio.share: It appears that collusion peaks at middle values of the room between cost and the walk-away spread, and that the preferenced share raises it by a similar amount at every room level. This fits the preferenced share acting only on the temptation to cheat, while the room acts on how visible collusion is to the screen and how many price steps a grid leaves. Without a grid, collusion most likely falls steadily with room; the rise from the narrowest room comes from grid markets needing space above normal competitive prices.
phi__sBarRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity peaks at a fairly narrow, but not the narrowest, room for every preferenced share, and that preferencing adds a similar amount throughout. The decline at wider rooms seems to be because the same degree of collusion becomes a wider spread that the screen notices, while the low value at the narrowest room most likely reflects grid markets with little or no space to raise prices.

tick__slope.share: It appears that collusion falls with both the tick size and the sensitivity of the screen, and that they reinforce each other. With no screen a fine grid makes little difference, but as the screen steepens the grid markets fall much faster. Without a grid, a cartel can most likely choose a tiny markup that the screen barely notices; with a grid, the smallest markup is a full price step that the screen always sees. This gap survives when the model's price-grid quirk is switched off, so it appears to be mainly genuine, with a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid adding to it.
tick__slope.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with both the tick size and the screen's sensitivity. For a fine grid, most of the shortfall compared with no grid seems to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid, because it vanishes when every investigation ends in a conviction. For a coarse grid, intensity stays lower even then, most likely because whole price steps stop the cartel from choosing a modest price that would escape the screen.

tick__rhoTip.share: It appears that collusion falls as tips become more likely and as the tick size grows, and that tips hurt proportionally more in grid markets. In markets without a grid, a tip costs expected fines and a shorter cartel life. In grid markets, a tip that finds no evidence most likely also wipes out ordinary competitive earnings, which appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid; when every investigation ends in a conviction, tips hurt about equally with or without a grid.
tick__rhoTip.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with both the tip probability and the tick size. The market without a grid is least affected by tips, most likely because there the cartels that still form respond to tips by pricing higher, since hiding helps little when a whistleblower may expose them anyway, which partly offsets the cartels lost.

tick__pEvidence.share: It appears that collusion falls with the tick size and, on average, as evidence becomes more likely. Without a grid, evidence acts as pure deterrence, because it raises the expected fine, so collusion falls steadily. With a grid the curve flattens and even turns up when evidence is certain, which appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid: an investigation that finds nothing ends ordinary earnings for good, while a conviction only costs the fine, so more evidence looks less bad.
tick__pEvidence.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls as the tick size grows and as evidence becomes more likely. Without a grid, intensity falls steadily with evidence, most likely because only the expected fine, the chance of conviction combined with the fine, matters. With a coarse grid it bottoms out and rises slightly when evidence is certain, which seems to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid.

tick__fineRatio.share: It appears that collusion falls steeply with the fine and with the tick size, and that fines bite much harder in grid markets. With no fine a fine grid makes little difference. Without a grid, a cartel can most likely pick a markup so small that the expected fine stays below its extra profit; with a grid, the smallest markup is a full price step, so the fine cannot be watered down that way.
tick__fineRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with the fine at every tick size, and falls faster in grid markets at low and middle fines. Under very heavy fines the tick sizes converge, most likely because the cartels that remain are mostly in scenarios with no screen and no tips, which never face a fine and so are unaffected by the grid's limits.

tick__sBarRatio.share: It appears that collusion falls with the tick size and peaks at middle values of the room between cost and the walk-away spread. Without a grid, collusion falls as the room widens, most likely because the same degree of collusion becomes a wider spread that the screen notices. With a coarse grid and the narrowest room, collusion is impossible, because normal competition on the grid already reaches the customers' walk-away spread. As the room widens the grid becomes small relative to it and the tick sizes converge.
tick__sBarRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with the tick size and peaks at a fairly narrow, but not the narrowest, room. Without a grid, intensity falls steadily as the room widens, apparently because the screen sees the wider spread. With a coarse grid and the narrowest room there is no collusion at all, and with a finer grid the only option there is a jump straight to the full-collusion price.

slope__rhoTip.share: It appears that collusion falls as the screen becomes more sensitive and as tips become more likely, but these act as substitutes. A tip does most damage where there is no screen and little where a steep screen already dominates, most likely because either is enough to start an investigation that ends the cartel. With no screen and no tips nothing can trigger an investigation, so the chart there shows simply where the cartel can be held together.
slope__rhoTip.theta: It appears that average collusion intensity falls with both the screen's sensitivity and the tip probability. Where there is a screen, tips seem to push the cartels that still form towards higher prices, because hiding from the screen helps little when a whistleblower may expose them anyway; the average still falls because fewer cartels form. With no screen, colluding firms most likely go straight to the full-collusion price, so tips lower intensity only by reducing how many cartels form.

slope__pEvidence.share: It appears that collusion falls as the screen becomes more sensitive and as evidence becomes more likely, and that these reinforce each other: evidence matters much more under a steeper screen. This is most likely because the screen creates investigations while evidence decides how costly each investigation is. The small upturn when evidence is certain under steep screens appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid; without a grid, collusion falls steadily.
slope__pEvidence.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with screen sensitivity and with the chance of finding evidence, at every level of each. More evidence most likely raises the expected fine attached to each extra bit of price. The slight upturns when evidence is certain under steep screens appear to be the same price-grid quirk rather than a real effect.

slope__fineRatio.share: It appears that collusion falls as the screen becomes more sensitive and as fines grow, and this is the strongest interaction in the model. What seems to matter is the screen and the fine together: a gentle screen with a heavy fine deters about as much as a steep screen with a moderate fine. With no screen the fine works only through tips, so many cartels survive even heavy fines, but a steep screen combined with a heavy fine makes collusion all but disappear.
slope__fineRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with both the screen's sensitivity and the fine. Without a screen, even a very heavy fine leaves noticeable intensity, most likely because the surviving cartels there face no risk of investigation and push prices to the full-collusion level. Even with no fine, a screen alone lowers intensity, apparently because an investigation ends the cartel's future profits, so cartels trade some margin for a longer life.

slope__sBarRatio.share: It appears that collusion falls as the screen becomes more sensitive and, on average, peaks at middle values of the room between cost and the walk-away spread. The inputs interact: with no screen, collusion rises with room, most likely only because grid markets need space above normal competitive prices, but with a screen, a wider room hurts because the same degree of collusion becomes a wider spread the screen notices. In effect, a wide room seems to act like a steeper screen.
slope__sBarRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with the screen's sensitivity and, on average, peaks at a fairly narrow, but not the narrowest, room. With no screen, intensity rises as the room widens, apparently from extra space on the price grid alone. Under a steep screen it falls as the room widens, most likely because a wider room makes the same degree of collusion more visible, so a screen in a wide market behaves like a steeper screen in a narrow market.

rhoTip__pEvidence.share: It appears that collusion falls as tips become more likely and as evidence becomes more likely, and that these compound: evidence deters more when tips are common. This is most likely because a tip can start an investigation at any price, so the risk of conviction applies whatever the cartel does, not only at high prices. The fall at the highest evidence levels is weaker than it would otherwise be, which appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid.
rhoTip__pEvidence.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with both the tip probability and the chance of finding evidence. Evidence most likely lowers intensity directly, since it raises the expected fine attached to each extra bit of price. Tips seem to lower intensity on average only because fewer cartels form, even though the cartels that remain tend to price higher.

rhoTip__fineRatio.share: It appears that collusion falls with both the tip probability and the fine, and that together they can end collusion entirely. A tip creates a minimum expected fine that no pricing choice can avoid, so once tips are common and fines are heavy, the expected fine most likely exceeds even the best profit a cartel could earn. Without tips, some collusion survives heavy fines, apparently in scenarios with no screen, where nothing ever triggers an investigation.
rhoTip__fineRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with the fine and with the tip probability, reaching nothing when tips are common and fines are heavy. With no fine, tips barely change intensity, most likely because a tip then only shortens the cartel's life: some cartels no longer form, but those that remain price higher, and these roughly cancel.

rhoTip__sBarRatio.share: It appears that tips lower collusion at every room level, proportionally more when the room between cost and the walk-away spread is narrow, and that collusion peaks at middle room values. Tips most likely matter more at narrow rooms because the screen sees only a small spread there, so a tip becomes the main way an investigation starts. The middle peak seems to blend a falling pattern in markets without a grid, where wider rooms are more visible to the screen, with grid markets needing space above normal prices.
rhoTip__sBarRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity peaks at a fairly narrow, but not the narrowest, room at every tip level, and that tips lower it throughout. Beyond the peak, a wider room most likely makes collusion more visible to the screen, while tips seem to lower the average mainly by reducing how many cartels form.

pEvidence__fineRatio.share: It appears that collusion falls with both the chance of finding evidence and the fine, because together they set the expected cost of each investigation; in markets without a grid a low chance of evidence with a heavy fine deters about as much as certain evidence with a lighter fine. With no fine, however, collusion rises with the chance of evidence even though nothing is ever fined, which appears to be a quirk of how the model treats markets with a price grid. Under heavy fines a small remnant of collusion remains, most likely in scenarios where no investigation can ever start.
pEvidence__fineRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls with the fine and, on average, with the chance of finding evidence, which together set the expected cost of an investigation. Once fines are meaningful, more evidence lowers intensity sharply. With no fine, intensity instead rises with evidence, which seems to be the same price-grid quirk rather than real behaviour.

pEvidence__sBarRatio.share: It appears that collusion falls as evidence becomes more likely at every room level, and peaks at middle values of the room between cost and the walk-away spread; the peak shifts slightly towards narrower rooms when evidence is certain. In markets without a grid collusion most likely falls steadily as the room widens, because a wider room means a more visible spread and a heavier fine relative to the profit from a small markup. The rise from the narrowest room appears to come from grid markets needing space above normal prices.
pEvidence__sBarRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity peaks at a fairly narrow, but not the narrowest, room for every evidence level, and falls as evidence becomes more likely. In markets without a grid, intensity seems to fall steadily in both directions: more evidence raises the expected fine, and a wider room makes the same collusion more visible to the screen.

fineRatio__sBarRatio.share: It appears that collusion falls steeply as fines grow and, on average, peaks at middle values of the room between cost and the walk-away spread. With no fine, collusion rises with the room, most likely only because grid markets need space above normal prices. With a fine, wider rooms become less attractive, apparently because the fine is measured against full-collusion profit, which grows with the room faster than the profit from a small, inconspicuous markup. Under the heaviest fines collusion is low at every room level.
fineRatio__sBarRatio.theta: It appears that collusion intensity falls as fines grow and peaks at a fairly narrow, but not the narrowest, room at every fine level. Without a grid, intensity seems to fall steadily as the room widens even with no fine, most likely because the screen judges the absolute spread, so the same degree of collusion looks more suspicious in a wide market. Under heavy fines the room levels converge on low intensity.
